questions.question: What does the feedback runner force the agent to do?
options: React to facts: structured stdout/stderr/exit/duration records captured on every command
Skip running the acceptance command entirely and report the previous turn's already-recorded exit code
Guess the outcome from the command's name and report that guess as the recorded result
Ask a separate model to imagine plausible output and log that imagined output instead
questions.explanation: The runner closes the gap between 'tests passed' (imagined) and 'tests actually ran and exited zero' (recorded).

questions.question: How does feedback differ from telemetry?
options: Telemetry only stores exit codes and timestamps, while feedback stores the full stdout and stderr text
Telemetry is written by the shell itself, while feedback is written by the model's own tokens
Feedback is for the next turn of this run; telemetry is for operators reviewing runs over time
Feedback records are encrypted at rest by default, while telemetry records are stored in plain text
questions.explanation: Both share fields but live in different files with different retention; feedback is intra-run, telemetry is cross-run.

questions.question: Which field MUST appear in every feedback record?
options: duration_ms, because a slow command is treated the same as a failed one by the loop
started_at, because records without a timestamp cannot be sorted into a retry chain
exit_code, since a null exit code must refuse to let the loop advance to its next turn
agent_note, because the loop cannot resume without the agent's own written expectation of the result
questions.explanation: exit_code is the unambiguous success signal; null exit means no progress.

questions.question: How does the runner truncate large outputs?
options: Deterministic head and tail truncation with a marker, so the same output always yields the same record
Random line sampling across the full output so large logs stay statistically representative
Keeping only the first ten lines of any command output, no matter where the actual failure occurs in the run
Compressing the full output with gzip and storing the compressed bytes inside the record
questions.explanation: Deterministic truncation keeps records replayable while bounding token cost; tails carry the failure summary.

questions.question: Why redact at write time rather than read time?
options: Write-time redaction runs faster than read-time redaction because it skips the regex pattern matching
The file on disk is what an attacker reaches; read-time redaction leaves secrets sitting in the JSONL file
Read-time redaction is impossible in practice because JSONL files cannot be parsed more than once
Write-time redaction is required by the JSON Schema that validates every feedback record before it is appended
questions.explanation: Redact lines matching Bearer, password=, api_key=, AKIA..., xox[baprs]- before append; auditing the patterns quarterly.

questions.question: What does parent_command_id give the workbench?
options: Faster subprocess spawning, since the runner can skip re-reading argv on every retry
A retry chain: retries link to their parent attempt so the failure history stays visible
A lower token cost per turn, since the field lets the agent skip reading stdout_tail
A smaller on-disk record, since the parent field replaces the need to separately store the command's argv
questions.explanation: Parent linkage makes retry chains visible to the reviewer (Lesson 39) and the verification gate.
